newsitem.title: BELGIUM: BELGIUM DE FACTO IN EMU WITH 1997 BUDGET - DEHAENE.
newsitem.headline: BELGIUM DE FACTO IN EMU WITH 1997 BUDGET - DEHAENE.

text.p: The Belgian government on Tuesday presented its 1997 budget which it believes will guarantee entry into Europe's economic and monetary union in 1999.
"Thanks to this budget, our country will comply with the Maastricht Treaty criteria for monetary union," Prime minister Jean-Luc Dehaene said in a speech to parliament.
At a news conference afterwards Dehaene was even more self-assured: "With this budget we are de facto members of EMU. We no longer need to realise this target, it has been achieved."
Belgium's 1997 budget aims to cut the total public sector deficit to 2.9 percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP), from an estimated 3.3 percent in 1996.
To do this, the goverment has decided on an austerity package worth 80 billion Belgian francs ($2.5 billion). One half consists of tax increases and the other half spending cuts.

Among the main tax measures are a 7.3 billion franc increase in petrol taxes, a 3.7 billion franc tax increase on beer, a four billion franc tax on the physical delivery of securities and a four billion franc tax on company cars.
In the social security sector the government has slashed 19.6 billion francs off health care spending.
Federal spending is cut by 17 billion francs, by reducing subsidies to the postal system and publicly-owned companies.
Dehaene also announced an unprecedented state debt reduction package, which aims to slice 370 billion francs off the country's 9,828 billion franc debt mountain.
The main measure is a 222 billion franc buyback of foreign debt, funded with central bank capital gains on gold sales in recent years.

A second part will come from sales of public assets worth 70 billion, including 25 billion from the sale of a further 25 percent stake in ASLK-CGER bank to Belgian-Dutch insurance and banking group Fortis.
Finally, the government also plans to earn 75 billion francs by investing public authorities' financial assets in state bonds rather than depositing them with banks.
The debt package, which has been okayed by the European Monetary Institute, is neutral for the budget, as the state will no longer earn interest on the central bank's capital gains.
But it will reduce Belgium's debt to GDP ratio -- the highest in Europe -- to 127.0 percent in 1997 from 130.4 percent in 1996 and 137.0 percent in 1993.
"Thus the debt ratio will have fallen by 10 percent in a four-year period," Dehaene said.

Dehaene reminded parliamentarians that before the summer they gave his government special powers to rule by decree until mid-1997 so that any measures would have immediate force of law without parliamentary approval, a luxury no other EU leader has had in the run-up to EMU.
"If for any reason, such as an economic slowdown, the budget threatens to veer off track, we can take immediate corrective measures using executive decrees," Deputy Prime Minister Elio di Rupo said.
Analysts and opposition politicians criticised the budget, which they said lacked vision and again delayed long-awaited fundamental reform of the social security system.
"It's a patchwork budget," said Peter Praet, chief economist at Belgium's biggest bank Generale Bank.
"The government is muddling along. What we need are drastic reforms," said Guy Verhofstadt, politician for the opposition VLD Flemish liberal party and a former budget minister.
But Christer Lindholm at J.P. Morgan in Brussels said the budget was "certainly good enough" to get Belgium into EMU.
Others also praised the conservative growth and interest rate forecasts on which the budget is based.
($1=31.36 Belgian Franc)
